title: Reliable rescue oxygenation in the difficult airway

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a fast, dependable way to restore oxygen delivery when conventional airway management has failed, usable across a substantially broader range of difficult-airway situations with practical equipment and training requirements. It could be a technology, a technique or an integrated rescue approach; the supplied evidence does not identify a completed solution. The clinical need is grounded in the 2022 American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) guidelines, which recognize difficulties or failures in mask ventilation, supraglottic ventilation, tracheal intubation and invasive airway access.

The immediate goal is rescue oxygenation, which does not always require placing a tube in the trachea. The guideline describes rescue ventilation through supraglottic airways as well as invasive alternatives. However, restoring oxygenation does not by itself establish sustained ventilation, adequate carbon dioxide clearance or protection against material entering the lungs. Those functions require separate assessment when deciding whether a rescue method can support the patient beyond the initial emergency.

significance.text: If a broadly usable rescue method could rapidly restore effective oxygenation after conventional approaches fail, with acceptable harms, it could interrupt progression toward brain injury, cardiopulmonary arrest and death. These are among the serious adverse outcomes identified in the ASA guideline. The potential safety benefit is therefore clinically grounded, but neither the fraction of injuries preventable by such an innovation nor the magnitude of its benefit is quantified by the supplied evidence.

Impact synthesis: Revolutionary significance would depend on a large improvement in both reliability and applicability over existing rescue pathways. A modest improvement to one device in a narrow patient group would not establish the broader capability described here. Success in most difficult-airway situations is a hypothetical ambition, not an observed success rate, and rapid initial oxygenation would have limited value if support could not be maintained long enough to stabilize the patient or establish subsequent care.

Conditional downstream possibility: A practical rescue capability could also improve safety in emergency medicine and critical care, including settings with different staff, equipment and access constraints. Those benefits would require validation in the intended settings. Evidence from anesthetic airway management alone cannot establish equivalent effectiveness across every emergency or critical-care population, and a rescue method would still need to fit into a pathway for sustained respiratory support and airway protection.

missing_breakthrough.text: The proposed unsolved capability is dependable rescue oxygenation despite a broad range of anatomical and physiological difficulties. The documented barriers include anatomy that makes even front-of-neck airway access difficult or unsuccessful, and patients whose condition makes interruption of breathing poorly tolerated. The ASA framework explicitly anticipates that a selected invasive approach may fail or be infeasible and calls for an alternative. This establishes the rescue challenge in the documented 2022 framework; it does not establish that no broader solution exists as of November 2026.

Engineering synthesis: A convincing advance would have to provide effective oxygen delivery quickly, maintain support for a clinically useful duration, accommodate substantial anatomical variation and remain usable under emergency conditions. Its failure modes would need to be recognizable early enough to permit another intervention. If the method is intended to provide ventilation as well as oxygenation, carbon dioxide clearance must also be adequate; if it provides only temporary oxygenation, the transition to further support becomes part of the practical problem.

Proposed scope requiring investigation: Trauma, bleeding and restricted access remain useful challenging scenarios for development and evaluation, but the supplied review did not find direct support in the retained guideline text for the original assertion that each defeats multiple conventional techniques. Their inclusion should therefore be treated as a proposed coverage goal. Feasible training, equipment availability and performance across different users are likewise requirements to be demonstrated, rather than established properties of an existing innovation.

current_state.text: The 2022 ASA Practice Guidelines for Management of the Difficult Airway, by Jeffrey L. Apfelbaum, Carin A. Hagberg and colleagues, document a framework using multiple alternatives. The narrative recommendations reviewed in the supplied material cover awake and anesthetized strategies, alternative devices and invasive rescue. They also anticipate failure of selected rescue approaches and recommend identifying alternatives. This is evidence of an established safety framework with contingency planning, rather than a demonstration of one universally successful technique.

The guideline reports case-level observations of successful rescue ventilation and intubation using supraglottic airways in unanticipated and emergency difficult airways. It also describes a retrospective observational study in which rescue transtracheal jet ventilation restored oxygen saturation to above 90%. These findings provide technical precedent for rescue oxygenation through existing methods. The supplied review does not provide the study's sample size, success proportion or duration of support, so the saturation threshold cannot be interpreted as a broad reliability estimate or evidence of improved neurological outcomes.

The evidence available here is historically bounded. The supplied review confirmed the guideline's identity from its internal bibliographic information, but its retained text stops during printed page 51 of an article spanning pages 31–81. The algorithms on printed pages 57–59 cited in the earlier candidate were outside that extract. The narrative recommendations support the dated account above, while the missing pages limit what can be claimed about the algorithms themselves.

Evidence limitation: No freshness assessment was supplied to establish the state of practice or the continued absence of the proposed capability as of November 2026. The source index records retrieval on November 11, 2026, but retrieval does not update the clinical content of a 2022 guideline. The supplied material therefore establishes neither achievement of this innovation nor its present-day absence. This limitation is not evidence that the reported rescue results are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: Independent clinical studies should show a substantial improvement in successful rescue oxygenation and clinically meaningful patient outcomes compared with prespecified contemporary difficult-airway pathways. Protocols should define the intended population, comparator, success criteria and meaning of substantial improvement before evaluation. The guideline's inclusion of restoration of failed oxygenation, complications and serious patient outcomes provides a clinical basis for these endpoints; the proposed evaluation requirements are not established completion standards endorsed by that source.
completion_criteria.label: Independent clinical studies demonstrate substantial rescue oxygenation and outcome improvements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed performance assessment: Studies should report time to effective oxygenation, duration of effective support, failures, complications and anatomical exclusions. Where the method is intended to provide sustained respiratory support, evaluation should also measure ventilation and carbon dioxide clearance and assess airway protection separately. Any temporary oxygenation role should have an explicit boundary and a demonstrated transition to subsequent support. Numerical thresholds remain to be defined for the intended use; none are supplied here as accepted standards.
completion_criteria.label: Report rescue support performance, safety and intended-use boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth and reproducibility assessment: Realistic simulation should test challenging scenarios across users, levels of experience and care settings, including the training time and equipment needed to achieve reliable performance. Independent teams and sites should reproduce the relevant findings. Simulation can reveal operational weaknesses and assess scenario coverage, but improved patient outcomes must be demonstrated clinically rather than inferred from simulated success.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce reliable performance across realistic difficult-airway simulations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: A convincing result should identify where the method works, where it fails, how quickly failure can be recognized and what fallback remains available. Evidence from a finite set of patients and scenarios establishes demonstrated breadth within those conditions. It cannot prove success in every patient or justify describing the capability as literally universal.
completion_criteria.label: Identify operating limits, failure recognition speed and available fallback

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ANS-04, Surgical unconsciousness with preserved breathing and circulatory control, shares the aim of maintaining physiological safety during anesthesia. Its focus is preserving breathing and circulation during surgical unconsciousness, whereas ANS-08 addresses oxygenation rescue after airway management fails. Preserved breathing would not itself guarantee oxygen delivery through an obstructed airway. ANS-06, Broad, active reversal of general anesthesia, concerns reversal of the anesthetic state; such reversal could complement some rescue pathways but would not by itself establish a dependable route through a difficult airway.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-05, A radically accessible, resilient anesthesia platform for essential surgery, overlaps with ANS-08 through equipment, training and deployment requirements. An effective rescue capability could be a component of such a platform, while the platform's broader accessibility would not establish rescue performance. Surgical airway access and extracorporeal support are also relevant areas of technical overlap identified in the review, but no supplied evidence establishes either as the broadly reliable solution proposed here.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-01, A causal theory of anesthetic-induced unconsciousness, and ANS-02, A reliable real-time monitor of conscious experience during anesthesia, concern the mechanisms and assessment of consciousness. ANS-08 instead concerns restoration of oxygen delivery during airway failure. These advances could coexist within safer anesthetic care, but neither a theory of unconsciousness nor a consciousness monitor demonstrates rescue oxygenation.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-03, A broadly applicable, pain-selective surgical nerve block; ANS-07, Systemic, non-opioid analgesia for severe perioperative pain; and ANS-09, Mechanism-based prevention of chronic postsurgical pain, address distinct aspects of pain control or prevention. Their advances could influence anesthetic choices, but their completion would not establish the airway rescue capability of ANS-08. These entries remain separate because analgesia, pain prevention and oxygenation rescue have different primary targets and demonstrations.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-10, Mechanism-guided anesthesia to prevent postoperative brain dysfunction, shares a broad concern with neurological outcomes. ANS-08 targets the specific emergency pathway of failed oxygenation that can cause brain injury. Successful rescue oxygenation would not establish prevention of postoperative brain dysfunction from other mechanisms, and progress on ANS-10 would not establish reliable difficult-airway rescue.

change_log.reason: Success at one respiratory function does not establish the others, which affects both clinical significance and completion criteria.

change_log.change: Integrated the reported supraglottic rescue observations and restoration of saturation above 90% with their evidentiary limits.
change_log.reason: These are useful technical precedents, but the supplied material does not establish broad reliability, duration of support or neurological benefit.

change_log.reason: The earlier algorithm citations on pages 57–59 fall outside the retained text, which stops during printed page 51.

unresolved_issues: Whether later evidence or technologies establish the proposed capability, or materially change its scope, remains unknown from the supplied material.
The method, intended patient populations, settings and anatomical exclusions have not been specified.
The full trauma, bleeding and restricted-access scenario claims remain insufficiently substantiated by the reviewed extract.
The underlying rescue studies' sample sizes, success proportions, complications and duration of effective support are not available in the supplied review.
Clinically meaningful improvement thresholds, appropriate contemporary comparators and the required duration of rescue support remain to be defined.
The preventable burden of neurological injury and death, and effectiveness in emergency and critical-care settings, remain unquantified.
The cited algorithms and later portions of the guideline were outside the retained extract; their contents cannot be resolved from the supplied review.

brief.title: Reliable oxygen rescue when breathing support fails
possible: When a mask or breathing tube cannot deliver enough oxygen, clinicians could have a fast, dependable rescue option. It would work across a much wider range of difficult situations, with practical equipment and training.
The rescue could keep oxygen flowing long enough to stabilize the patient or establish further breathing support.
why: Patients could avoid brain injury, cardiac arrest and death when ordinary ways of supporting breathing fail. Clinicians would gain a more dependable way through an emergency in which each failed attempt costs time.

sources.who: Jeffrey L. Apfelbaum, Carin A. Hagberg and colleagues
sources.showed: Their clinical guidelines describe several rescue options and report cases in which existing methods restored oxygen delivery. They also anticipate that a chosen rescue method may fail.
sources.cited_for: Existing methods can rescue oxygen delivery, while difficult anatomy can defeat even access through the neck.
sources.not_established: The guidelines do not demonstrate a broadly dependable rescue method or quantify its benefit to patients.

sources.showed: A retrospective study linked a windpipe tube (ETI) to better oxygen delivery and carbon dioxide removal after prolonged cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), attempts to restart the heart.
sources.quote: ETI was associated with improved oxygenation and ventilation after prolonged CPR.
sources.cited_for: The study supports assessing oxygen delivery, carbon dioxide removal and patient outcomes separately.
sources.not_established: This observational comparison does not demonstrate dependable rescue after conventional airway methods fail.

sources.who: Secdegül Coşkun Yaş, Emel Altıntaş, Ayfer Keleş and Ahmet Demircan
sources.showed: In a mannequin study involving 24 residents, a flexible guide helped clinicians place a breathing tube through a neck incision on the first attempt more often than the traditional surgical method.
sources.quote: The success rate of the bougie-guided cricothyrotomy in the first attempt was higher than that of the traditional surgical technique.
sources.cited_for: The study demonstrates an improvement in one simulated difficult-airway situation.
sources.not_established: A small mannequin study cannot establish reliable oxygen rescue or better outcomes in patients.

shown: The American Society of Anesthesiologists guidelines describe successful rescues using devices above the voice box and oxygen delivered through the neck. These are examples of rescue working, rather than a measure of reliability across difficult situations.

Secdegül Coşkun Yaş and colleagues improved first-attempt tube placement in a mannequin designed to simulate obesity. Overall success and procedure time did not differ significantly between the methods.
missing: Independent clinical studies still need to demonstrate substantially better rescue success and patient outcomes than current care.
A rescue method still needs to demonstrate fast oxygen delivery that lasts long enough for stabilization or further support.
Broad reliability still needs to be demonstrated across difficult anatomy, users and settings, with practical training and equipment.

milestones.label: Independent studies demonstrate better rescue and patient outcomes
milestones.explanation: Independent clinical studies would have to show substantial gains over current rescue pathways using criteria set beforehand. This would establish that the approach improves patient care.

milestones.label: Studies establish support duration, safety and intended uses
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to measure speed, duration, harms and exclusions, plus carbon dioxide removal and lung protection where intended. This would establish how long rescue can safely support a patient.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce reliable performance in realistic simulations
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce reliable simulation results across users, experience levels and settings, documenting training and equipment needs. This would test practical breadth.

milestones.label: Operating limits and fallback options become clear
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to establish where the method fails, how quickly failure is recognized and which fallback remains available. This would define its safe operating limits.

uncertain: The rescue method, intended patients and care settings remain unspecified.
The required improvement, appropriate comparison and necessary duration of support remain undefined.
Restoring oxygen alone does not establish adequate carbon dioxide removal or protection against material entering the lungs.

page.title: Rescue oxygenation in cannot-intubate, cannot-oxygenate emergencies
page.definition: A rescue approach restores blood oxygenation in adults after tracheal intubation, mask ventilation and ventilation through a supraglottic airway—a device above the voice box—have failed. Comparative clinical evidence establishes greater rescue success than the relevant guideline pathway within a specified patient population.

goal.need: NAP4 attributed 46 deaths or persistent brain injuries to airway events among 184 reported major complications. Rescue oxygenation addresses an observed cause of death and neurological injury. This audit of selected severe events does not estimate how many outcomes a new rescue method would prevent.

figures.caption: Outcomes among 184 major airway events reported to the UK NAP4 audit
figures.note: Events occurred from 1 September 2008 to 31 August 2009 in anaesthesia, intensive care and emergency departments. These counts are not population incidence estimates.

statements.context: A recommendation for unanticipated and emergency difficult-airway management.

statements.quote: The recommendations prioritise continuous oxygen delivery throughout airway management;
statements.context: The opening priority in the guidelines’ summary; the guidelines were published online in 2025.

completion.title: Independent clinical evidence reproduces superior oxygenation rescue after conventional airway failure.
completion.criterion: A comparative clinical study demonstrating greater rescue-oxygenation success than contemporary guideline-based rescue care is independently replicated in the same defined adult indication after failed intubation, mask ventilation and supraglottic ventilation. Both studies meet their prespecified efficacy and safety endpoints. Their oxygenation endpoints cover stabilization or transition to definitive respiratory support. The demonstrated capability is limited to the populations and settings studied.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body’s general completion threshold was located.
completion.basis: Searches covered ASA 2022 and DAS 2025 guidance, NAP4, rescue-device regulatory records, standards and clinical-trial registries for a general success probability, rescue-time limit, support duration or comparative efficacy threshold. None was found. Replicated clinical superiority within a defined indication is the narrowest test that distinguishes the proposed advance from the clinical rescues already documented.

milestones.title: A rescue airway ventilates an obese manikin within three attempts of at most 180 seconds each.
milestones.criterion: In the published obese-airway manikin protocol, successful cricothyrotomy requires inflation of the balloon representing the lung during manual bag ventilation. Each attempt is stopped after 180 seconds; three attempts are allowed per technique. The study published on 8 November 2024 included 24 residents and reported that 23 succeeded with both techniques. This establishes simulated airway access and ventilation, not blood oxygenation.
milestones.set_by: Coşkun Yaş and colleagues, published manikin-study methods; a study-specific test for surgical cricothyrotomy.
milestones.threshold_quote: The procedure was considered successful if the balloon representing the manikin’s lung was inflated during artificial manual (Ambu) bag ventilation.

milestones.title: Rescue ventilation restores pig arterial oxygen saturation >95% and carbon dioxide <45 mmHg within 1 minute.
milestones.criterion: The published porcine protocol requires arterial oxygen saturation above 95% and arterial carbon dioxide partial pressure below 45 mmHg within one minute of starting rescue ventilation. Six anaesthetized pigs had complete upper-airway obstruction except for a 100 cm catheter with a 3 mm internal diameter; rescue began after apnoeic desaturation to approximately 70% by pulse oximetry. Ventrain restored oxygenation and normocarbia within one minute in all six pigs; ventilation continued for ten minutes.
milestones.set_by: de Wolf and colleagues, published porcine-study primary aim; a study-specific test of Ventrain through an airway exchange catheter.
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary aim was to assess whether efficient oxygenation (SaO2 > 95%) and ventilation (PaCO2 < 45 mmHg) could be restored within one minute.

milestones.title: A rescue method restores patients’ oxygen saturation above 90% during difficult intubation.
milestones.criterion: The clinical study defines successful rescue transtracheal jet ventilation as pulse-oximeter oxygen saturation above 90% during jet ventilation. Its retrospective series, covering March 2001 through September 2011, reported effective rescue in 31 patients, including 26 with upper-airway cancer, and one case of subcutaneous emphysema without pneumothorax. The series demonstrates clinical rescue under this definition; it does not establish comparative effectiveness or require failure of every conventional oxygenation route.
milestones.set_by: Bouroche and colleagues, published retrospective-study methods at Institut Gustave-Roussy; the definition was written for transtracheal jet ventilation.
milestones.threshold_quote: Success of emergency RTTJV was deﬁned when SpO2 was > 90% under jet ventilation.

milestones.title: A prospective clinical comparison demonstrates greater oxygenation-rescue success than guideline care.
milestones.criterion: A prospective comparative study in a defined adult population after failed intubation, mask ventilation and supraglottic ventilation demonstrates superiority over contemporary guideline-based rescue care for its prespecified oxygenation-success endpoint and meets its prespecified safety endpoints. Successful oxygenation extends through stabilization or transition to definitive respiratory support. This is the initial comparative clinical demonstration awaiting independent replication.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback after searches of guidelines, regulatory records and trial registries found no general comparative clinical milestone for this capability.

not_found: No outside body’s general threshold for rescue success probability, time to oxygenation or duration of support was located.
No prospective comparative study with independent replication was located that establishes the completion criterion.
